ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Shown in the diagram is a graph of $f'$, the derivative of function $f$. If $f(3)=3$, then $f(1)=$?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: What is given in the figure is the graph of f'; it is a straight line, passing through the point (0,-2) on the y-axis, and intersects the x-axis at x=3, that is, it passes through (3,0). Therefore on the interval [1,3], f' is below the x-axis, and f'(1)=-4/3, f'(3)=0. Then reason: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, f(3)-f(1)=\int_1^3 f'(x)\,dx. The signed area on the interval [1,3] is the area of the triangle below the x-axis, with base 2 and height 4/3, so the integral value is -\frac12\cdot 2\cdot \frac43=-\frac43. Therefore 3-f(1)=-\frac43, solving gives f(1)=3+\frac43=\frac{13}{3}.
